claim: VMP1 is an ER transmembrane protein essential for autophagy and certain types of secretion.
source: Here, we show that the release of lipoproteins from the ER membrane requires VMP1, an ER transmembrane protein essential for autophagy and certain types of secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work on VMP1's role in autophagy and secretion.

claim: Loss of vmp1 in zebrafish causes lipoprotein accumulation in the intestine and liver.
source: Loss of vmp1, but not other autophagy-related genes, in zebrafish causes lipoprotein accumulation in the intestine and liver.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Vmp1 deficiency in mice leads to lipid accumulation in the visceral endoderm and intestine.
source: Vmp1 deficiency in mice also leads to lipid accumulation in the visceral endoderm and intestine.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: In VMP1-depleted cells, neutral lipids accumulate within lipid bilayers of the ER membrane.
source: In VMP1-depleted cells, neutral lipids accumulate within lipid bilayers of the ER membrane, thus affecting lipoprotein secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7.

claim: VMP1 is important for the release of lipoproteins from the ER membrane to the ER lumen.
source: These results suggest that VMP1 is important for the release of lipoproteins from the ER membrane to the ER lumen in addition to its previously known functions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lipoproteins are primarily formed in and secreted from the intestine, liver, and visceral endoderm.
source: Lipoproteins are primarily formed in and secreted from the intestine, liver, and visceral endoderm (Farese et al., 1996; Sirwi and Hussain, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Neutral lipids are synthesized and accumulate within the lipid bilayer of the ER membrane at an early stage in lipoprotein assembly.
source: At an early stage in lipoprotein assembly, neutral lipids are synthesized and accumulate within the lipid bilayer of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane (Demignot et al., 2014; Sundaram and Yao, 2010; Tiwari and Siddiqi, 2012; Yen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: MTTP is an ER luminal chaperone that interacts, stabilizes, and lipidates APOB.
source: This step requires microsomal triglyceride-transfer protein (MTTP), an ER luminal chaperone that interacts, stabilizes, and lipidates APOB (Sirwi and Hussain, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: VMP1 was originally identified as a pancreatitis-associated protein.
source: Vacuole membrane protein 1 (VMP1), which was originally identified as a pancreatitis-associated protein, is a multispanning membrane protein in the ER (Dusetti et al., 2002; Vaccaro et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: VMP1 (EPG-3 in Caenorhabditis elegans) is essential for autophagosome formation in mammals, Dictyostelium, and Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: VMP1 (EPG-3 in Caenorhabditis elegans) is essential for autophagosome formation in mammals (Itakura and Mizushima, 2010; Ropolo et al., 2007; Tian et al., 2010), Dictyostelium (Calvo-Garrido et al., 2008), and Caenorhabditis elegans (Tian et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: VMP1 controls ER contact with other membranes, including autophagic membranes.
source: VMP1 also controls ER contact with other membranes, including autophagic membranes (Tábara and Escalante, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017), by regulating the calcium pump sarcoendoplasmic reticulum calcium transport ATPase (SERCA) (Zhao et al., 2017) and ER contact proteins VAPA and VAPB (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: VMP1 is required for the secretion of soluble proteins that are transported via the ER-to-Golgi trafficking pathway.
source: In addition to the involvement in autophagy, VMP1 is known to be required for the secretion of soluble proteins that are transported via the ER-to-Golgi trafficking pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In Drosophila S2 cells, VMP1 (identified as TANGO5) is important for constitutive secretion and Golgi organization.
source: In Drosophila S2 cells, VMP1 (identified as TANGO5) is important for constitutive secretion and Golgi organization (Bard et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In Dictyostelium, VMP1 is required for secretion of specific proteins such as α-mannosidase and a cysteine proteinase.
source: In Dictyostelium, VMP1 is required for secretion of specific proteins such as α-mannosidase and a cysteine proteinase and maintenance of organelle homeostasis (Calvo-Garrido et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: VMP1 is essential for survival under hypoosmotic and starvation conditions in Dictyostelium and Caenorhabditis elegans, respectively.
source: Physiologically, VMP1 is essential for survival under hypoosmotic and starvation conditions in Dictyostelium (Calvo-Garrido et al., 2008) and Caenorhabditis elegans (Tian et al., 2010), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Neutral lipid-containing structures accumulate in VMP1-depleted cells.
source: Recent studies in human cells (Morita et al., 2018; Tábara and Escalante, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017) and Caenorhabditis elegans (Zhao et al., 2017) revealed that neutral lipid-containing structures accumulate in VMP1-depleted cells, suggesting the function of VMP1 in lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A frameshift mutation was introduced into exon 6 of the vmp1 gene in zebrafish using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: A frameshift mutation was introduced into exon 6 of the vmp1 gene (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The abdominal part was less transparent in vmp1-/- zebrafish at 6 days post fertilization (dpf), indicating the presence of abnormal deposits.
source: Gross examination revealed that the abdominal part was less transparent in vmp1-/- zebrafish at 6 days post fertilization (dpf), indicating the presence of abnormal deposits (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The swimbladder was not inflated in vmp1-/- zebrafish.
source: We also noticed that the swimbladder was not inflated in vmp1-/- zebrafish, which will be described in more detail elsewhere.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: All vmp1-/- zebrafish died around at nine dpf.
source: All vmp1-/- zebrafish died around at nine dpf (Figure 1C), suggesting that VMP1 is essential for survival during the larval period.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VMP1 is essential for survival during the larval period in zebrafish.
source: All vmp1-/- zebrafish died around at nine dpf (Figure 1C), suggesting that VMP1 is essential for survival during the larval period.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that all vmp1-/- zebrafish died around 9 dpf.

claim: Autophagy was defective in vmp1-/- zebrafish.
source: Autophagy was defective in vmp1-/- zebrafish; many large LC3 puncta accumulated in several tissues, including the brain, spinal cord, and skeletal muscles, which were abnormal autophagy-related structures typically observed in VMP1-deficient mammalian cells (Itakura and Mizushima, 2010; Kishi-Itakura et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2017) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1D, with supporting citations.

claim: An increase in the levels of the lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II) was observed in vmp1-/- zebrafish.
source: An increase in the levels of the lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II) was also observed in vmp1-/- zebrafish (Figure 1E), as previously observed in VMP1-deficient mammalian cells (Itakura and Mizushima, 2010; Morita et al., 2018; Shoemaker et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E, with supporting citations.

claim: Autophagic flux is blocked in vmp1-/- zebrafish.
source: These results suggest that autophagic flux is blocked in vmp1-/- zebrafish.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the accumulation of LC3 puncta and increased LC3-II levels.

claim: The abnormal deposits in the abdomen were observed in all vmp1-/- zebrafish (n = 11), but not in vmp1+/- (n = 30) or vmp1+/+ zebrafish (n = 7).
source: The abnormal deposits in the abdomen were observed in all vmp1-/- zebrafish (n = 11), but not in vmp1+/- (n = 30) or vmp1+/+ zebrafish (n = 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with specific sample sizes.

claim: The deposits in vmp1-/- zebrafish were stained with oil red O, a neutral lipid-soluble dye.
source: Indeed, the deposits in vmp1-/- zebrafish were stained with oil red O, a neutral lipid-soluble dye (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In vmp1-/- zebrafish, large neutral lipid-containing structures accumulated in intestinal epithelial cells and hepatocytes.
source: Oil red O staining of cross sections and electron microscopy revealed that, in vmp1-/- zebrafish, large neutral lipid-containing structures accumulated in intestinal epithelial cells and hepatocytes (Figure 2B,C) but not in other organs, including the brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B) and skeletal muscles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and supplementary figures.

claim: Accumulation of large lipid-containing structures was not observed in zebrafish lacking the rb1cc1/fip200 or atg5 gene.
source: Accumulation of large lipid-containing structures was not observed in zebrafish lacking the rb1cc1/fip200 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) or atg5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) gene, both of which are required for autophagy (Hara et al., 2008; Mizushima et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in supplementary figures, with supporting citations.

claim: The lipid phenotype in vmp1-/- zebrafish is not caused by deficient autophagy.
source: These results suggest that neutral lipids accumulate in vmp1-/- zebrafish, and that this lipid phenotype is not caused by deficient autophagy.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that rb1cc1-/- and atg5-/- zebrafish do not show the same lipid accumulation phenotype.

claim: Vmp1gt/gt embryos were detected at 7.5 days postcoitum (dpc) but not after 9.5 dpc.
source: In contrast, Vmp1gt/gt embryos were embryonic lethal; they were detected at 7.5 days postcoitum (dpc) but not after 9.5 dpc (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Vmp1gt/gt embryos at 7.5 dpc were smaller than wild-type embryos and accumulated the autophagy substrate p62.
source: Vmp1gt/gt embryos at 7.5 dpc were smaller than wild-type embryos and accumulated the autophagy substrate p62 (Figure 3B), suggesting that VMP1 is important for early embryonic development as well as autophagy in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: VMP1 is important for early embryonic development as well as autophagy in mice.
source: Vmp1gt/gt embryos at 7.5 dpc were smaller than wild-type embryos and accumulated the autophagy substrate p62 (Figure 3B), suggesting that VMP1 is important for early embryonic development as well as autophagy in mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the embryonic lethality and p62 accumulation in Vmp1gt/gt embryos.

claim: The visceral endoderm is an extraembryonic layer critical for maternal-to-embryo transfer of nutrients such as neutral lipids between 5 and 10 dpc, before the placenta is formed.
source: The visceral endoderm is an extraembryonic layer critical for maternal-to-embryo transfer of nutrients such as neutral lipids between 5 and 10 dpc, before the placenta is formed (Bielinska et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Visceral endoderm cells secrete lipoproteins to the epiblast, an embryonic layer.
source: Like intestinal epithelial cells and hepatocytes, visceral endoderm cells secrete lipoproteins to the epiblast, an embryonic layer (Farese et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Neutral lipids accumulated in visceral endoderm cells in Vmp1gt/gt embryos at 7.5 dpc.
source: Indeed, neutral lipids accumulated in visceral endoderm cells in Vmp1gt/gt embryos at 7.5 dpc (Figure 3C), as observed in vmp1-deficient zebrafish intestinal epithelial cells and hepatocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Vmp1flox/flox;Villin-Cre mice weighed less than Vmp1flox/+;Villin-Cre mice.
source: Vmp1flox/flox;Villin-Cre mice weighed less than Vmp1flox/+;Villin-Cre mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Accumulation of p62 was observed in intestinal epithelial cells in 3-month-old Vmp1flox/flox;Villin-Cre mice.
source: Accumulation of p62 was observed in intestinal epithelial cells in 3-month-old Vmp1flox/flox;Villin-Cre mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The intestines of 8-month-old Vmp1flox/flox;Villin-Cre mice showed accumulation of neutral lipids within intestinal epithelial cells.
source: The intestines of 8-month-old Vmp1flox/flox;Villin-Cre mice showed accumulation of neutral lipids within intestinal epithelial cells (Figure 3F), suggesting a conserved function of VMP1 in the intestine.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: VMP1 has a conserved function in the intestine.
source: The intestines of 8-month-old Vmp1flox/flox;Villin-Cre mice showed accumulation of neutral lipids within intestinal epithelial cells (Figure 3F), suggesting a conserved function of VMP1 in the intestine.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of similar phenotypes in zebrafish and mice.

claim: In the serum from Vmp1flox/flox;Villin-Cre mice, the levels of cholesterol and lipoproteins such as high density lipoprotein (HDL) decreased compared to those from Vmp1flox/+;Villin-Cre mice.
source: In the serum from Vmp1flox/flox;Villin-Cre mice, the levels of cholesterol and lipoproteins such as high density lipoprotein (HDL) decreased compared to those from Vmp1flox/+;Villin-Cre mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: VMP1 is critical for homeostasis of neutral lipids and lipoproteins in a whole body.
source: These results suggest that VMP1 is critical for homeostasis of neutral lipids and lipoproteins in a whole body.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decreased serum cholesterol and lipoprotein levels in intestinal epithelial cell-specific Vmp1-deficient mice.

claim: In VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells, the amount of triglyceride and cholesterol decreased in culture media.
source: In VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells, the amount of triglyceride and cholesterol decreased in culture media (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: In VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells, the intracellular amounts of triglyceride and cholesterol increased.
source: In contrast, the intracellular amounts increased (Figure 4A,B), suggesting that the secretion of neutral lipids depends on VMP1.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: The secretion of neutral lipids depends on VMP1.
source: In contrast, the intracellular amounts increased (Figure 4A,B), suggesting that the secretion of neutral lipids depends on VMP1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decreased extracellular and increased intracellular neutral lipids in VMP1-silenced cells.

claim: Knockdown of VMP1 reduced the amount of APOB in culture media.
source: Likewise, knockdown of VMP1 reduced the amount of APOB in culture media (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Knockdown of VMP1 reduced the amount of intracellular APOB.
source: Paradoxically, it also reduced the amount of intracellular APOB (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The reduction of intracellular APOB in VMP1-silenced cells was likely due to enhanced degradation of misfolded APOB by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: This was likely due to enhanced degradation of misfolded APOB by the ubiquitin-proteasome system because treatment with lactacystin, a proteasome inhibitor, restored the amount of intracellular APOB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: VMP1 is critical not only for APOB homeostasis but also for the secretion of lipoproteins.
source: These results suggest that VMP1 is critical not only for APOB homeostasis but also for the secretion of lipoproteins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reduced extracellular APOB even after proteasome inhibition.

claim: Secretion of APOE was impaired in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells.
source: Secretion of APOE, a component of very low density lipoprotein (VLDL), and APOA-I, a component of HDL, was also impaired in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Secretion of APOA-I was affected only slightly in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells.
source: Secretion of APOA-I was affected only slightly.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Secretion of albumin was not significantly impaired in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells.
source: In contrast, secretion of albumin, which is transported from the ER to Golgi separately from lipoproteins (Tiwari and Siddiqi, 2012), was not significantly impaired in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C, with a supporting citation.

claim: Secretion of collagens was not affected by VMP1 deletion.
source: Secretion of collagens, another type of large cargo that requires TANGO1 for secretion (Saito et al., 2009), was not affected by VMP1 deletion because cartilage structures, which are composed of collagens secreted from cartilage cells, was normal in vmp1-/- zebrafish (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in supplementary figures, with a supporting citation.

claim: A defect in secretion in VMP1-deficient cells is not general, but rather specific to lipoproteins.
source: Thus, a defect in secretion in VMP1-deficient cells is not general, but rather specific to lipoproteins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that albumin and collagen secretion are not affected while lipoprotein secretion is impaired.

claim: In vmp1-/- zebrafish, almost all large lipid-containing structures in intestinal epithelial cells and hepatocytes were surrounded by the ER transmembrane protein Sec61B.
source: In vmp1-/- zebrafish, almost all large lipid-containing structures in intestinal epithelial cells and hepatocytes were surrounded by the ER transmembrane protein Sec61B (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In most cases, Sec61B covered only a part rather than all of the surface of the lipid structures in vmp1-/- zebrafish.
source: In most cases, Sec61B covered only a part rather than all of the surface of the lipid structures.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: In Vmp1gt/gt mouse embryos, almost all neutral lipid-containing structures were positive for SEC61B.
source: Also, in Vmp1gt/gt mouse embryos, almost all neutral lipid-containing structures were positive for SEC61B (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neutral lipid structures in vmp1+/- animals were mostly negative for Sec61B/SEC61B.
source: In contrast, neutral lipid structures in these tissues in vmp1+/- animals were mostly negative for Sec61B/SEC61B, suggesting that they are present outside the ER, most likely as cytosolic lipid droplets (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Neutral lipids abnormally accumulate in the ER in vmp1-deficient zebrafish and mouse tissues.
source: Thus, neutral lipids abnormally accumulate in the ER in vmp1-deficient zebrafish and mouse tissues.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SEC61B staining data.

claim: In vmp1-/- zebrafish, most of the lipid-containing structures were positive for ApoB.
source: In vmp1-/- zebrafish, most of the lipid-containing structures were positive for ApoB (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The lipid structures were mostly positive for APOB in Vmp1gt/gt mouse embryos.
source: In addition, the lipid structures were mostly positive for APOB in Vmp1gt/gt mouse embryos (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Most lipid structures in vmp1+/- animals were ApoB/APOB-negative.
source: In agreement with SEC61B staining data, most lipid structures in these tissues in vmp1+/- animals were ApoB/APOB-negative (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Lipoproteins or lipoprotein-related structures are formed and accumulate in VMP1-deficient cells.
source: These results suggest that lipoproteins or lipoprotein-related structures are formed and accumulate in VMP1-deficient cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the APOB staining data.

claim: In wild-type HepG2 cells, neutral lipid structures were mostly positive for ADRP but negative for APOB.
source: In wild-type HepG2 cells, neutral lipid structures were mostly positive for adipose differentiation-related protein (ADRP, also known as perilipin 2), a marker for cytosolic lipid droplets, but negative for APOB irrespective of oleic acid treatment that increased the number of lipid-containing structures (Figure 6A–C), suggesting that these are lipid droplets rather than lipoproteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 6A-C.

claim: Large lipid structures accumulated in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells and most of them were APOB positive.
source: In contrast, as shown in zebrafish and mice (Figure 5), large lipid structures accumulated in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells (Figure 6A) and most of them were APOB positive (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 6A and 6C.

claim: Some lipid structures in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells were positive for both APOB and ADRP, where APOB and ADRP were distributed into distinct regions.
source: Some of them were positive for both APOB and ADRP, where APOB and ADRP were distributed into distinct regions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: APOB- and ADRP-double positive structures represent structures stuck within the ER lipid bilayers facing both the cytosol and the ER lumen, rather than those released into the ER lumen.
source: They should represent structures stuck within the ER lipid bilayers facing both the cytosol and the ER lumen, rather than those released into the ER lumen (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the APOB and ADRP staining pattern, supported by a model in Figure 6D.

claim: APOE, but not APOA-I, colocalized with APOB on the lipid structures in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells.
source: APOE, but not APOA-I, colocalized with APOB on the lipid structures in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells (Figure 6E,F), suggesting that the defective secretion of APOB and APOE (Figure 4C) is at least partly caused by trapping in the lipid structures.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: The defective secretion of APOB and APOE is at least partly caused by trapping in the lipid structures.
source: APOE, but not APOA-I, colocalized with APOB on the lipid structures in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells (Figure 6E,F), suggesting that the defective secretion of APOB and APOE (Figure 4C) is at least partly caused by trapping in the lipid structures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the colocalization of APOE and APOB on lipid structures.

claim: The ER membranes with ribosomes on their cytosolic face covered a part of the surface of the lipid structures in vmp1-/- zebrafish intestinal epithelial cells and hepatocytes.
source: Electron microscopy of intestinal epithelial cells (Figure 7A) and hepatocytes (Figure 7B) of vmp1-/- zebrafish and VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells (Figure 7C) revealed that the ER membranes with ribosomes on their cytosolic face covered a part of the surface of the lipid structures (Figure 7A–C, black arrowheads) and fused with the lipid structures at both ends (Figure 7A–C, white arrowheads).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: The space between the ER membrane and the lipid structures should be the ER lumen.
source: The space between the ER membrane and the lipid structures should be the ER lumen (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electron microscopy data, supported by a model in Figure 7D.

claim: Lipid accumulation within the ER membrane was not observed in vmp1+/- zebrafish and wild-type HepG2 cells.
source: In contrast, lipid accumulation within the ER membrane was not observed in vmp1+/- zebrafish and wild-type HepG2 cells (Figure 7A–C, arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: In hepatocytes in vmp1+/- zebrafish, there was no membrane on large lipid structures, which should represent cytosolic lipid droplets.
source: In hepatocytes in vmp1+/- zebrafish, there was no membrane on large lipid structures, which should represent cytosolic lipid droplets (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: VMP1 is important for the release of lipoproteins into the ER lumen.
source: These results suggest that neutral lipids abnormally accumulate within the lipid bilayer of the ER membrane in the absence of VMP1, and VMP1 is important for the release of lipoproteins into the ER lumen (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the electron microscopy data, supported by a model in Figure 7D.

claim: The ER protein VMP1 has a novel nonautophagic function in the release of lipoproteins from the ER membrane into the lumen.
source: Based on the findings in this study, we propose that the ER protein VMP1 has a novel nonautophagic function in the release of lipoproteins from the ER membrane into the lumen (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the discussion, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: The step of lipoprotein release from the ER membrane is distinct from the exit from the ER.
source: This step is distinct from the exit from the ER; it is generally thought that intraluminal lipoproteins are transported to the Golgi (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a model in Figure 7D.

claim: The phenotype of deletion of VMP1 is different from that of factors required for lipoprotein export from the ER lumen to the Golgi.
source: Consistently, the phenotype of deletion of VMP1 is different from that of factors required for lipoprotein export from the ER lumen to the Golgi (Figure 7D); deletion of TANGO1, TALI (Santos et al., 2016), cTAGE5 (Wang et al., 2016), or SURF4 (Saegusa et al., 2018) does not cause an accumulation of large lipid-containing structures in human hepatocellular carcinoma cells or epithelial colorectal adenocarcinoma cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: VMP1 is important for the release of lipid droplets from the ER membrane to the cytosol.
source: Our results also suggest that VMP1 is important for the release of lipid droplets from the ER membrane to the cytosol because the number of ADRP-positive lipid droplets decreased in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 6A and 6C.

claim: VMP1 may regulate a common process shared by the three pathways derived from the ER: autophagy, lipoprotein formation, and lipid droplet formation.
source: Thus, VMP1 may regulate a common process shared by the three pathways derived from the ER: autophagy, lipoprotein formation, and lipid droplet formation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: VMP1 might regulate remodeling of the ER membrane.
source: One hypothesis is that VMP1 might regulate remodeling of the ER membrane.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: The release of neural lipid-containing structures from the ER membrane to the ER lumen or the cytosol would require drastic reorganization of the membrane.
source: The release of neural lipid-containing structures from the ER membrane to the ER lumen or the cytosol would require drastic reorganization of the membrane (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a logical inference stated in the discussion, supported by a model in Figure 7D.

claim: During autophagy, the ER membranes dramatically change their shapes and contact with the autophagic membranes.
source: In addition, during autophagy, the ER membranes dramatically change their shapes and contact with the autophagic membranes (Hayashi-Nishino et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Without VMP1, expansion of the autophagic membranes is defective.
source: Without VMP1, expansion of the autophagic membranes is defective (Kishi-Itakura et al., 2014; Morita et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: VMP1 is essential for survival during larval periods and early embryonic periods in zebrafish and mice, respectively.
source: In this study, we showed that VMP1 is essential for survival during larval periods and early embryonic periods in zebrafish and mice, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: Vmp1-deficient mice died around at 8.5 dpc.
source: Vmp1-deficient mice died around at 8.5 dpc.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: The timing of lethality of Vmp1-deficient mice is earlier than that of mice deficient for other core autophagy-related genes such as Rb1cc1, Atg13, and Atg5.
source: This timing of lethality is earlier than that of mice deficient for other core autophagy-related genes such as Rb1cc1, Atg13, and Atg5 (Kuma et al., 2017; Mizushima and Levine, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: One of the causes of the early embryonic lethality of Vmp1-deficient mice is likely malabsorption of lipids from maternal blood.
source: Considering the early embryonic lethality of ApoB- or Mttp-deficient mice around at 10.5 dpc due to malabsorption of lipids from maternal blood (Farese et al., 1995; Farese et al., 1996; Raabe et al., 1998), one of the causes of the early embryonic lethality of Vmp1-deficient mice is likely the same mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the discussion, based on comparison with other mutant mice.

claim: The reduction of body weight and levels of serum cholesterol and lipoproteins in intestinal epithelial cell-specific Vmp1-deficient mice indicates defects in the absorption of nutrients.
source: The reduction of body weight (Figure 3D) and levels of serum cholesterol and lipoproteins (Figure 3G) in intestinal epithelial cell-specific Vmp1-deficient mice indicates defects in the absorption of nutrients.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 3D and 3G.

claim: Intestinal epithelial cell-specific Vmp1-deficient mice showed milder phenotypes in lipoprotein secretion compared to intestinal epithelial cell-specific Mttp-deficient mice.
source: In contrast to intestinal epithelial cell-specific Mttp-deficient mice (Iqbal et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2006), intestinal epithelial cell-specific Vmp1-deficient mice showed milder phenotypes in lipoprotein secretion; the level of serum triglyceride did not decrease in intestinal epithelial cell-specific Vmp1-deficient mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations and data in Figure 3G.

claim: Although VMP1 is important, it is not absolutely essential for lipoprotein secretion.
source: Thus, although VMP1 is important, it is not absolutely essential for lipoprotein secretion.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the discussion based on the milder phenotype compared to Mttp-deficient mice.

claim: Two independent genome-wide association studies in humans identified intronic single-nucleotide polymorphism associations (rs11650106 and rs2645492) in the VMP1 gene with altered levels of circulating LDL.
source: Two independent genome-wide association studies in humans identified intronic single-nucleotide polymorphism associations (rs11650106 and rs2645492) in the VMP1 gene with altered levels of circulating LDL (Chu et al., 2012; Hoffmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: VMP1 may be important for the regulation of the levels of circulating lipoproteins in humans.
source: Thus, VMP1 may be important for the regulation of the levels of circulating lipoproteins in humans.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the discussion based on genome-wide association studies.

claim: Lipoproteins are composed of a neutral lipid core (triglycerides and cholesterol esters) surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer and proteins (called apolipoproteins).
source: Lipoproteins are composed of a neutral lipid core (triglycerides and cholesterol esters) surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer and proteins (called apolipoproteins).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Lipid structures are associated with apolipoprotein B (APOB), a major protein constituent of lipoproteins, co-and/or post-translationally.
source: These lipid structures are associated with apolipoprotein B (APOB), a major protein constituent of lipoproteins, co-and/or post-translationally (Davidson and Shelness, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Lipoproteins are released into the ER lumen and transported to the Golgi for secretion.
source: Then, lipoproteins are released into the ER lumen (Demignot et al., 2014; Sundaram and Yao, 2010; Tiwari and Siddiqi, 2012; Yen et al., 2015) and transported to the Golgi for secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: How lipoproteins bud off from the ER membrane to the ER lumen remains largely unknown.
source: A key long-standing question is how lipoproteins bud off from the ER membrane to the ER lumen, which remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: VMP1 forms ER subdomains enriched in phosphatidylinositol synthase at ER-autophagic membrane contact sites.
source: At the ER-autophagic membrane contact sites, VMP1 forms ER subdomains enriched in phosphatidylinositol synthase (Tábara et al., 2018), which could serve as the initiation site of autophagosome formation (Nishimura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: VMP1 is required for secretion of specific proteins such as α-mannosidase and a cysteine proteinase in Dictyostelium.
source: In Dictyostelium, VMP1 is required for secretion of specific proteins such as α-mannosidase and a cysteine proteinase and maintenance of organelle homeostasis (Calvo-Garrido et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Chromatographic analysis revealed significant reductions in lipoproteins such as very low-density lipoproteins and low-density lipoproteins in the culture media of VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells both under normal and oleic acid-treated conditions.
source: Chromatographic analysis using different detection methods for neutral lipids also revealed significant reductions in lipoproteins such as very low-density lipoproteins and low-density lipoproteins in the culture media of VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells both under normal and oleic acid-treated conditions, the latter of which stimulates lipoprotein secretion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Treatment with lactacystin, a proteasome inhibitor, restored the amount of intracellular APOB in VMP1-silenced cells.
source: This was likely due to enhanced degradation of misfolded APOB by the ubiquitin-proteasome system because treatment with lactacystin, a proteasome inhibitor, restored the amount of intracellular APOB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The amount of extracellular APOB remained lower in VMP1-silenced cells than that in control cells even after lactacystin treatment.
source: Nevertheless, the amount of extracellular APOB remained lower in VMP1-silenced cells than that in control cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Secretion of VSVG, a glycoprotein of vesicular stomatitis virus, is normal in vmp1/epg-3 mutant Caenorhabditis elegans and VMP1 knockout COS7 cells.
source: This result is consistent with a previous report that showed the secretion of collagens and model cargo proteins such as VSVG, a glycoprotein of vesicular stomatitis virus, is normal in vmp1/epg-3 mutant Caenorhabditis elegans and VMP1 knockout COS7 cells, respectively (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: In VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells, proteasome activity was not suppressed.
source: In VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells, however, proteasome activity was not suppressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment of wild-type HepG2 cells with proteasome inhibitors (MG132 or lactacystin) did not induce crescent-shaped accumulations of APOB and ADRP.
source: In addition, treatment of wild-type HepG2 cells with proteasome inhibitors (MG132 or lactacystin) did not induce crescent-shaped accumulations of APOB and ADRP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Neither ER stress nor reduced MTTP protein level was observed in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells.
source: However, neither ER stress (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) or reduced MTTP protein level (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) was observed in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Treatment of wild-type HepG2 cells with ER stress inducers (tunicamycin or thapsigargin) did not induce the crescent-shaped accumulations of APOB and ADRP.
source: Treatment of wild-type HepG2 cells with ER stress inducers (tunicamycin or thapsigargin) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B) or an MTTP inhibitor (CP-346086) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) did not induce the crescent-shaped accumulations of APOB and ADRP.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The crescent-shaped accumulations of APOB and ADRP were not observed in HepG2 cells deficient for FITM2.
source: Furthermore, the crescent-shaped accumulations of APOB and ADRP were not observed in HepG2 cells deficient for FITM2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D,E), a factor required for budding of lipid droplets from the ER membrane to the cytosol, but not for lipoprotein secretion (Choudhary et al., 2015; Goh et al., 2015; Kadereit et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in supplementary figures, with supporting citations.

claim: The crescent-shaped accumulations of APOB and ADRP in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells is not due to proteasome inhibition, ER stress, MTTP suppression, or defective budding of lipid droplets from the ER membrane.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the crescent-shaped accumulations of APOB and ADRP in VMP1-silenced HepG2 cells is not due to proteasome inhibition, ER stress, MTTP suppression, or defective budding of lipid droplets from the ER membrane.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple negative control experiments.

claim: VMP1 could play a possible role in lipid metabolism.
source: Since the release of lipoproteins and lipid droplets from the ER membrane can be regulated by lipid metabolism such as phospholipid remodeling (Ben M'barek et al., 2017; Wang and Tontonoz, 2019), VMP1 could play a possible role in lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion with supporting citations.
